items.title: DeepMind introduces AlphaProof Code, an AI system that generated three million lines of formal proofs in Lean to verify Signal's core encryption [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
items.summary:
DeepMind has developed AlphaProof Code, an AI agent capable of producing extensive formal proofs to verify complex software systems. The system wrote three million lines of proofs in the Lean theorem prover to validate the security of Signal's core encryption.

This breakthrough demonstrates the potential of AI to assist in deep software verification tasks, improving the reliability and security of critical cryptographic software. The approach could pave the way for more automated and rigorous software assurance in security-sensitive applications.

items.title: VulnCheck tracks 442 CVEs attributed to Anthropic's Project Glasswing with only two exploited in the wild, revealing a widening gap between vulnerability discovery and fixes
items.originalTitle: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
items.summary:
VulnCheck has monitored Anthropic's Project Glasswing for seven months, identifying 442 CVEs linked to the project, which represents about 0.5% of all CVEs published this year. Despite nearly 38,000 reported findings, only 7,349 have been made public and just 217 fixed, with only two vulnerabilities exploited in the wild, raising questions about the project's impact and effectiveness.

Since September, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 new findings but fixed only 15, while duplicates and withdrawn findings have increased significantly, suggesting challenges in managing and remediating reported vulnerabilities. Anthropic's claimed true positive rate has risen to 94.2%, but external validation, such as from the curl project, has disputed many reported vulnerabilities, further complicating the assessment of the project's accuracy and value.

items.title: Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and MDN teams launch Modern Web Guidance to help coding agents adopt modern web platform features over legacy JavaScript patterns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
items.summary:
Modern Web Guidance is a collaborative project by Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams that provides curated skills and best practices to steer coding agents away from outdated JavaScript toward modern web platform APIs. It offers a CLI tool that integrates expert guidance on browser compatibility, performance, accessibility, and native web features to improve code quality and efficiency.

The guidance covers recent web platform advancements including CSS layout, animations, native UI components, accessibility improvements, and built-in AI capabilities like on-device language detection and translation. It aims to reduce reliance on legacy code and heavy polyfills by promoting lightweight, platform-optimized solutions. The project includes tools to scan codebases for legacy patterns and retrieve targeted modernization advice, supporting developers in producing production-ready, modern web applications.

items.title: Engineer warns AI-generated codebases tend to be fragile due to shallow tests, complexity, reduced human understanding, and rapid changes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
items.summary:
A former Meta engineer who transitioned to fully AI-generated coding at a large tech company highlights that AI-assisted development often produces brittle codebases. The engineer notes that AI tends to write superficial tests, overly complex code, and accelerates development pace beyond human review capacity, leading to increased technical debt and fragility.

The engineer identifies four main issues with AI-generated code: shallow test coverage that misses critical cases, unnecessary complexity from rigid adherence to coding guidelines, diminished human understanding of the codebase, and faster pull requests that reduce review quality. These factors contribute to more frequent and prolonged incidents in production environments, raising concerns about the sustainability of AI-driven software development for large-scale SaaS applications.

items.title: Researcher explains reasoning in AI as pathfinding through token space, clarifying why longer chains of thought do not always improve accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What objective is reasoning solving?
items.summary:
The article presents a perspective on reasoning in AI models as a process of pathfinding through token space, where multiple paths can lead from a prompt to a correct answer. It challenges the intuitive idea that longer chains of thought always yield better results, noting that forcing longer reasoning chains can sometimes degrade accuracy. Instead, reasoning success depends on the probability of sampling paths that reach correct answers, which can be improved by training models to generate better paths or by sampling multiple paths and selecting the best.

The author illustrates this concept with examples and mathematical formulations, explaining how reinforcement learning maximizes the likelihood of finding successful paths rather than guaranteeing convergence on a single chain. This framework also helps explain phenomena like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking in reasoning models. The article suggests that increasing the number of sampled reasoning paths is a more reliable way to improve accuracy than simply extending the length of individual reasoning chains.

items.title: ZeroPoint introduces a fixed zero-energy state in energy-based decision models to enable explicit abstention decisions, improving option compatibility assessment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ZeroPoint: Lightweight Energy-Based Decision Model
items.summary:
ZeroPoint is a new energy-based model (EBM) that assigns a fixed zero energy to an empty answer state for every input, providing a clear reference point to decide whether any option fits. Unlike standard EBMs that only learn relative compatibility among options, ZeroPoint integrates the decision to select an option or abstain into ordinary inference, trained with negative log-likelihood loss, without requiring a separate rejection rule. The model uses a small multilingual encoder that processes the input and options invariant to their order.

Experiments show that training with examples where no option fits contributes most to the model's effectiveness. ZeroPoint's fixed zero state separates inputs with and without acceptable options better than a learned rejection class and significantly better than thresholded softmax, while maintaining consistent choice among options. This approach enhances decision-making in scenarios where abstention is a valid outcome.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to every joint value of the observed and predicted variables. In decision models, the prediction is chosen from a finite list of options provided with each input. Inference then reduces to comparing the energies of the options, and training lowers the energy of the correct option relative to the others. A complete decision must also account for the possibility that no option is acceptable. However, the energies learned by a standard EBM define only relative compatibility: adding the same input-dependent quantity to all energies leaves the predictions, the Gibbs distribution, and the usual training losses unchanged. The model therefore has no learned reference level against which to decide whether any option fits. We propose ZeroPoint, an EBM that makes the empty answer a state of the model with energy zero for every input. This fixed state provides an explicit reference for the energies of all listed options, whose non-negative depths measure their compatibility with the input relative to the empty answer. The options and the empty answer share one distribution, in which an option at zero depth receives no probability. The decision to select an option or to abstain is thus part of ordinary inference, trained with the negative log-likelihood loss, rather than a separate rejection rule. The energy function is a small multilingual encoder that reads the input together with all the options and is invariant to their order. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples in which no option fits. With the same encoder and data, the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax, while leaving the choice among options unchanged.

items.title: Researchers propose State-Conditional Invariance for reliable vision-language model judges and introduce GridWM-Judge benchmark revealing diverse failure modes in multimodal task evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Reliable VLM Judges: State-Conditional Invariance and Presentation-Aware Diagnostics
items.summary: Researchers propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a principle requiring vision-language model (VLM) judges to maintain stable verdicts under semantics-preserving presentation changes while responding to causal task outcome changes. They introduce GridWM-Judge, a diagnostic benchmark based on MiniGrid trajectories with variants testing perception, transitions, presentation stability, and causal discrimination. Evaluations reveal varied failure modes including sensitivity to evidence presentation, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak counterfactual discrimination, with visual grounding and objective recovery identified as key model-dependent challenges. The study suggests reporting correctness alongside presentation stability and causal sensitivity for more reliable VLM judge assessments.

Evaluations reveal varied failure modes including sensitivity to evidence presentation, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak counterfactual discrimination, with visual grounding and objective recovery identified as key model-dependent challenges. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for multimodal and embodied tasks, yet aggregate accuracy or consistency alone does not reveal whether a judge changes its verdict for the right reason. We propose State-Conditional Invariance (SCI), a reliability principle requiring a judge to remain stable under semantics-preserving changes in presentation while responding to causal interventions that change the task outcome. We instantiate SCI in GridWM-Judge, a simulator-grounded diagnostic benchmark built from deterministic MiniGrid trajectories with aligned Full, evidence-removal, and counterfactual variants, plus presentation and representation probes. Across five diagnostic tasks, GridWM-Judge tests local perception, action-conditioned transitions, presentation stability, representation exchangeability, and Full-CF causal discrimination. Our diagnostic evaluations reveal heterogeneous failure modes, including sensitivity to evidence presentation and encoding, low activation on successful trajectories, and weak paired counterfactual discrimination. Perception-controlled analyses further indicate that visual grounding and objective recovery are substantial, model-dependent bottlenecks. These results motivate jointly reporting correctness, presentation stability, and causal sensitivity instead of relying on a single score.

items.title: Study compares three evaluation frameworks for enterprise LLM analytics agents, assessing stability, known risk detection, and unknown failure discovery [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks—trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics—applied to two analytics agents using frozen execution traces. They found that 97% of configurations met stability thresholds, with the trace-based framework achieving the best precision-recall balance on known risk detection and text-only evaluation generating more false alarms. The study also uncovered 24 novel failures with no overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming, highlighting the complementary nature of these approaches.

The results indicate that the quality of evaluation depends on the information available to the harness, and that LLM-based evaluation can detect subtle errors missed by human reviewers. The authors recommend using a two-framework strategy combining trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation to improve reliability in enterprise analytics agent deployment.

items.title: Researchers introduce Contrastive Discovery method for LLM agents to resolve scientific questions by evaluating competing explanations, improving resolution rates across six domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
items.summary:
Researchers propose Contrastive Discovery, a method that replaces single hypothesis testing with contrast sets containing mutually exclusive competing explanations, allowing large language model (LLM) agents to better resolve scientific questions. This approach scores experiments based on how evidence redistributes belief among alternatives, enabling agents to identify which explanation the evidence supports rather than just rejecting one hypothesis.

In tests across six domains, Contrastive Discovery resolved 73% of rejected hypotheses to specific alternatives and increased question resolution by 67% compared to pointwise evaluation under the same experiment budget. A blinded study with 38 human experts showed high agreement with the method's resolved explanations, supporting its effectiveness in improving scientific discovery from existing evidence and validation resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

items.title: Researchers develop method to improve clinical documentation models by filtering actionable clinician edits to reduce hallucinations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Actionable Feedback: Improving Model Capabilities from User Edit Data on Clinical Documentation
items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in clinical documentation, where clinicians edit AI-generated outputs before use. Researchers found that over 45% of these edits add information not supported by the model's inputs, risking hallucinations if used for fine-tuning. To address this, they created a taxonomy of clinician editing behaviors based on real-world data and generated semi-synthetic edit data using the MIMIC-III dataset for discharge summaries. They introduced filtering methods to identify actionable edits, showing that naive fine-tuning on raw edits increases ungrounded content, while their filtering approach improves alignment with clinician expectations and maintains faithfulness to input context.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in clinical documentation workflows, where clinicians review and edit their outputs before use. In principle, these clinician edits represent a scalable source of supervision for model training. In practice, not all edits represent actionable feedback: for instance, on data drawn from real-world deployment of an AI clinical documentation product, our review suggests that over 45% of edited outputs contain user-added information that is not directly supported by the inputs to the model. Naively fine-tuning on such edits risks teaching the model to hallucinate. In this paper, we develop a method to address this challenge. Given that real clinician edits on deployed documentation tools are not publicly available, we first develop a taxonomy of clinician-editing behaviors, informed by data from a deployed AI clinical documentation product. Then, we develop a method for generating semi-synthetic clinician-edit data, informed by our taxonomy, on a discharge-summary generation task based on MIMIC-III, a public dataset. Finally, we introduce simple filtering methods for identifying actionable edits, with accuracy evaluated by expert review. We show empirically, on our semi-synthetic dataset, that naive fine-tuning on raw edited output increases ungrounded content, while our approach of progressively filtering toward grounded edits enables improvement on clinician-alignment metrics while retaining faithfulness to the input context.

items.title: Researchers propose Möbius Interaction Filtering for multimodal humor detection, achieving 70.6% accuracy on UR-FUNNY and demonstrating applicability to sentiment prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: M\"obius Interaction Filtering: Order-Selective Spectral Regularization for Multimodal Humor Detection
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Möbius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), a method that jointly interprets language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior for multimodal humor detection by regulating interaction orders through spectral regularization. MoIF uses private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interactions to build unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors aggregated via a Möbius-domain filter that controls higher-order contributions to prediction.

Experiments on the UR-FUNNY dataset show MoIF improves signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 to 2.79 times compared to co-trained trimodal predictors, achieving 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1, outperforming thirteen other methods. Evaluations on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI datasets confirm MoIF's applicability to sentiment prediction, with cross-seed analyses indicating more stable performance estimates. The approach links multimodal interaction organization to statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint, and the code is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.12913v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.

items.title: Researchers analyze when multi-temperature sampling improves large language model inference and find single tuned temperature often suffices in pass@K settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Temperature to Rule Them All?
items.summary: Researchers investigate the effectiveness of varying sampling temperatures during inference in large language models, focusing on the pass@K evaluation setting. They analyze success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, discovering that while multi-temperature schemes can improve performance, the gains over a well-tuned single temperature are generally modest. The study identifies that harder questions tend to require different temperatures, but this effect grows only logarithmically with difficulty. The authors introduce an efficient method to evaluate optimal multi-temperature allocations and explain the limited benefits through mathematical "dulling effects" that stabilize temperature choices across question distributions. Their findings clarify when temperature diversity is beneficial and provide guidance on selecting sampling temperatures for inference.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time sampling is a central mechanism for improving large language models, with temperature controlling the tradeoff between reliability and diversity. While recent work suggests that varying temperature across samples can improve multi-sample inference, simple fixed-temperature schemes remain the standard in practice. We investigate this discrepancy in the canonical pass@K setting, asking when temperature diversity is useful, and when a single tuned temperature suffices. To this end, we analyze per-question success probabilities across multiple models and datasets, tracking how they vary with sampling temperature. We identify several consistent properties of these profiles, including that harder questions are less likely to share efficient sampling temperatures, although this trend is only logarithmic in hardness. We then derive an efficient method for evaluating the theoretically optimal multi-temperature allocation scheme, and show that although such a scheme improves performance, its gains over single-temperature baselines are typically modest when temperature is tuned as a function of the sampling budget K. We explain this phenomenon through mathematical mechanisms that we call dulling effects, and show how they ensure the robustness of temperature choices across different question distributions. Our results clarify when multi-temperature sampling is useful, and how temperatures should ideally be chosen.

items.title: Researchers propose ASPIRE, a large language model agent framework for nonlinear system identification with iterative reasoning and exploration, validated on three physical systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASPIRE: An Agentic System-Identification Platform for Iterative Reasoning and Exploration
items.summary:
ASPIRE is a framework that uses a large language model agent to autonomously select and execute nonlinear system identification methods, constructing interpretable models from measured data with optional physical knowledge and requirements. The system operates interactively or autonomously, allowing iterative analysis and validation, and was tested on a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter, producing valid models in all 30 runs at low cost.

The evaluation showed that the models met most criteria for interpretation, structure selection, and parameter estimation, with some discrepancies related to unsupported claims about model structure selection. ASPIRE's approach aims to reduce the need for expert intervention in system identification by integrating formal verification and user interaction.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method. ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language. Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds. We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run. An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18. The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

items.title: Researchers propose action-sequence alignment using longest common subsequence to select compatible successful references for multi-turn on-policy distillation, improving performance on ALFWorld and airline benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Which Successes Make Good References? Action-Sequence Alignment for Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers address the challenge of selecting suitable successful trajectories as references for multi-turn on-policy distillation (OPD) in tool-use agents, where incompatible successes can mislead supervision. They model reference selection as an optimal transport problem and use action-sequence alignment via longest common subsequence (LCS) to measure compatibility between failed and successful trajectories, making compatibility the key criterion for reference selection.

Experiments on the ALFWorld environment and the airline domain of the \(\tau^3\)-bench demonstrate that LCS-based reference selection outperforms reference-free OPD across multiple metrics. Additionally, models trained with airline data transfer effectively to the retail domain, showing improvements without further optimization, highlighting the generalizability of the approach.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces train-inference distribution mismatch by supervising a student on its own trajectories. For multi-turn tool-use agents, conditioning the teacher on a validated same-task successful trajectory as a reference can provide useful hindsight, but different successes may reach incompatible interaction states and offer misleading supervision. We cast successful-reference selection as a free-target optimal transport problem, which reduces to assigning each failed trajectory its most compatible successful reference. Because latent state paths are hidden, we use action-sequence alignment as an observable proxy for compatibility and instantiate it with longest common subsequence (LCS), which identifies a shared ordered backbone of actions while allowing recoverable detours. This perspective makes trajectory compatibility the central criterion for reference selection in multi-turn OPD. Experiments on ALFWorld and the airline domain of $\tau^3$-bench show that LCS is the only evaluated reference selector to improve over reference-free OPD on both ALFWorld overall scores and all three airline metrics. Without further optimization, the airline-trained models also transfer to the retail domain, where LCS improves all three metrics.

items.title: Researchers propose sequence-level Rényi entropy from Sequential Monte Carlo decoding as a zero-cost uncertainty measure for adaptive large language model reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Free Lunch Uncertainty: Sequence-Level R\'enyi Entropy from Particle Decoding for Adaptive LLM Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers introduce a method to quantify uncertainty over entire large language model (LLM) completions using sequence-level Rényi entropy (SRE) derived from Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding, enabling selective prediction and adaptive compute without additional cost. This approach extends to a family of stepwise entropies and outperforms traditional log-probability signals in multiple settings, including the MATH500 benchmark.

The study demonstrates that the order-1/2 Rényi entropy accumulates per-step search effort and serves as the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in most tested scenarios. An 8-particle probe identifies tasks benefiting from more particles, and a two-pass policy achieves accuracy comparable to 64-particle decoding with 34.2% fewer particles, indicating efficiency gains in adaptive LLM reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying uncertainty over an entire LLM completion is critical for selective prediction and adaptive compute. Zero-cost signals such as mean token entropy and log-probability are local to tokens or to one completion, and self-consistency needs many extra completions. We show that Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) decoding for power sampling already estimates the normalizing constant of the power distribution, which gives the sequence-level R'enyi entropy (SRE) of the model's completion distribution at zero marginal cost, with a guarantee at every particle budget. A R'enyi chain rule extends this readout to a family of stepwise entropies of any order. We prove that orders above one are tied to the most likely token of each step, which explains why they track log-probability, while the order-1/2 member accumulates the log of per-step search effort. This member is the best zero-cost selective-prediction signal in 10 of 13 settings. On MATH500 its AUROC is 0.022 to 0.044 above log-probability with all four models and within length quartiles, and the same order is selected when each setting is held out. An 8-particle probe identifies the problems that benefit from more particles, and a two-pass policy matches 64-particle accuracy on MATH500 with 34.2% fewer particles over three seeds.

items.title: Researchers model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution for gaze-augmented reward training, improving preference prediction accuracy in language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers propose a method that integrates human eye-tracking data into reward model training for language models by modeling visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on gaze location. This approach builds on cognitive psychology findings about letter recognition and extends prior fixation-centric models to better align model outputs with human preferences.

Their experiments show that the reward model trained with this gaze distribution achieves higher accuracy in predicting preferences compared to baseline models. Some results align qualitatively with established knowledge of human attention during reading, suggesting the model captures meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

items.title: Synapse-Control introduces lightweight runtime control for large language model agents, improving task success by 29.8% and reducing inference costs compared to Sentry [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Synapse-Control: Making Agent Experience Actionable with Lightweight Runtime Control
items.summary:
Synapse-Control is a new agent runtime designed to enhance the reliability of large language model agents on complex tool-based tasks by reusing execution experience more efficiently. It uses a lightweight control plane with rules and a 1.7 billion parameter classifier to select relevant advice and decide when to send it to the task-executing model, avoiding costly generative failure diagnoses.

The system employs micro-contracts for reusable interface checks and a Prompt Value Table to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget constraints. In tests involving 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieved 270 successes—29.8% more than the baseline—while replacing 4,987 generative diagnosis calls and cutting auxiliary control time by about half compared to Sentry.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13615v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents reuse execution experience to improve reliability on complex tool-based tasks. Systems such as Sentry call large models to generate failure diagnoses before retrieving advice, adding inference cost to experience reuse. We present Synapse-Control, an agent runtime whose lightweight control plane selects advice and determines when to send it to the task-executing model. Rules shortlist relevant advice, and a lightweight 1.7B classifier fine-tuned on teacher-labeled state-suggestion pairs scores those candidates instead of generating a diagnosis. Micro-contracts encode reusable interface checks, such as required arguments or valid options, without prescribing complete task programs. A Prompt Value Table records earlier guidance and feedback to limit repeated suggestions through cooldown and token-budget checks. Across 1,308 attempts per method in AppWorld and WebShop, Synapse-Control achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively.

items.title: Researchers assess personalized privacy protection capabilities of 21 large vision-language models using SPY-Bench, finding low compliance and limited contextual understanding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
items.summary: Researchers evaluated 21 state-of-the-art large vision-language models (LVLMs) for their ability to enforce personalized privacy protections at inference time, using a new benchmark called SPY-Bench with 32,700 samples across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios. They found that most models performed poorly, with only about 24% compliance accuracy and limited understanding of contextual privacy instructions. To address this, the team developed initial alignment methods, including a Noise Contrastive Alignment variant that achieved 96.88% accuracy while maintaining general performance, marking a step toward more controllable and ethical LVLM deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.13997v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP$^3$), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP$^3$ ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP$^3$ ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only $\sim$24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP$^3$ alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/achernarwang/specify-privacy-yourself

items.title: Researchers introduce CAMP-II to train language-model agents on file-based memory for long-horizon tasks, achieving nearly 3x improvement over prior methods on CAMG-II environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: Researchers present Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), a method that trains a single policy across five long-horizon reinforcement learning environments to learn file-based memory behaviors using asynchronous on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher. CAMP-II enables agents to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements, significantly improving performance on the Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II) benchmark suite. The approach achieves 2.97 times the gain of the strongest previous baseline and generalizes to external benchmarks Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 with improved success rates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergencies can occur where there is no phone signal and no ambulance nearby. A small language model on a phone can be helpful in such situations, but its advice needs to be safe and accurate. We built HandsOnAid, a 4-bit Gemma 2B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on FirstAidQA dataset, a corpus of 5,550 first-aid question-answer pairs. We compared seven configurations, including the base, 4-bit and 8-bit fine-tuned models, and versions with a length floor, safety gate, or retrieval. We used a 41-pair question-answer bank with medically reviewed references that followed ANZCOR guidelines, and a strict 0-5 score rubric, with twelve safety overrides. Four frontier LLM judges (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3) blindly scored every answer, with 45 hidden controls used to check judge reliability. Fine-tuning improved the mean score by +1.08 over the base model to 2.34. The best configuration scored 2.51 out of 5 which was the fine-tuned 4-bit model with retrieval. A medical professional also conducted a blind evaluation of 40 answers across the base, the 4-bit fine-tuned, and the retrieval configurations, and the scores were similar to the LLM judges' average scores. A keyword audit found limited coverage of several details of ANZCOR guidelines in the training corpus, that are required by the rubric, which suggests that missing information in the training data could be a cause of the low scores. On a smartphone device (Pixel 7 Pro) with six CPU threads and no network connection, the 4-bit fine-tuned model produced its first displayable text in 6.86 seconds and a complete answer in 14.88 seconds on average over ten questions.

items.title: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10201v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

items.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
items.summary: arXiv:2601.21343v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are classically trained in stages: pretraining on raw text followed by post-training for instruction following and reasoning. However, this separation creates a fundamental limitation: many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new way to pretrain and mid-train models that incorporates these behaviors earlier. We utilize an existing strong, post-trained model to both rewrite data and to judge policy model rollouts, thus introducing thinking and reinforcement earlier in training. We further improve reasoning at all stages by introducing the concept of self-improving post-thinking: improving the model's reasoning and self-judging ability by reasoning after generation. In our experiments, we show these approaches can give strong gains across multiple axes.

items.title: Cold-Start Personalization via Bayesian Adaptive Questioning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cold-Start Personalization via Bayesian Adaptive Questioning
items.summary: arXiv:2602.15012v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cold-start personalization requires inferring preferences from minimal interaction when no user-specific historical data is available. The space of possible preferences is vast, yet users care about only a sparse subset and rarely articulate them upfront; combined with limited interaction budgets, this makes preference elicitation challenging. Our key insight is that preferences exhibit predictable structure across populations; e.g., users who want detailed explanations often also value worked examples. We propose CAPE (Cold-start Adaptive Preference Elicitation), which learns a structured world model of preference correlations offline from complete profiles, then performs training-free Bayesian inference online to select informative questions and predict complete preference profiles, including dimensions never asked about. Even simple belief model instantiations (e.g., linear regression) substantially outperform end-to-end RL. Across medical, mathematical, social, and commonsense reasoning, CAPE achieves 80.8% alignment with ground-truth user preferences versus 68.5% for RL, requires 2.5x to over 15x fewer interactions, and adapts its questions twice as often as RL. Our contribution is a principled decomposition of cold-start personalization that makes Bayesian preference elicitation practical at scale for LLM systems.

items.title: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Examining the Impact of Data and Training Methods on Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment
items.summary: arXiv:2605.12798v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Post-training a language model can induce surprising behavioral changes far beyond the intended training target. We study two particularly striking examples: emergent misalignment (EM), where fine-tuning on a narrow dataset leads to misaligned behavior in unrelated contexts, and subliminal learning (SL), where a student model inherits a teacher's misalignment through seemingly benign training data. We examine how the training data, evaluation data, and training method shape where and how strongly misalignment transfers between data and models. We characterize the data by the domain of a prompt (its topical context) and its task (the function the model performs), and we build natural-language and synthetic datasets organized as domain-task grids. We find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts that share the task of the fine-tuning data than to prompts that share its domain. In the synthetic setting, tasks that the model has learned well spread misalignment more broadly. For SL, we go beyond SFT (supervised fine-tuning) to off-policy distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution and, to our knowledge for the first time, on-policy distillation, where the teacher only scores tokens sampled by the student. Misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under SFT and at a level comparable to off-policy distillation. Unlike SFT, where the teacher both generates the data and supervises the student, distillation lets us separate the two. With the teacher fixed, the data change how much misalignment the student inherits, but the teacher determines to which domains and tasks it transfers most strongly. Together, these results show how data and training influence the extent and patterns of emergent and subliminal misalignment.

items.title: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Mediated Communication Can Steer Collective Opinion
items.summary: arXiv:2605.16245v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into the online platforms where humans exchange opinions; large language models (LLMs) have been polishing users' posts on LinkedIn and providing context for content shared on X. While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We address this gap via a combination of empirical and theoretical analyses. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. Building on this observation, we introduce a mathematical model of opinion dynamics in which an AI system sits between users on a social network, transforming the opinions they express and perceive. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.

While prior work has shown that AI can express biased opinions and shape individuals' opinions during human-AI interactions, less attention has been paid to its influence on collective opinion formation when mediating human-to-human communication. We address this gap via a combination of empirical and theoretical analyses. We show empirically that LLMs from multiple popular families introduce directional biases when instructed to edit human-written texts on contested topics, for example, nudging texts in favor of gun control and against atheism. Building on this observation, we introduce a mathematical model of opinion dynamics in which an AI system sits between users on a social network, transforming the opinions they express and perceive. By analytically characterizing the equilibrium of this model and performing simulations on real social network data, we show that biases introduced by AI in human-to-human communication can be amplified through the network and shift collective opinion in their direction. In light of these findings, we investigate whether such biases are controllable by online platforms. We audit the "Explain this post" feature on X and find evidence of pro-life bias in Grok's outputs on abortion-related content, which we trace back to specific design choices. We conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings in relation to ongoing legislative efforts in the European Union.

items.title: Pruning and Distilling Mixture-of-Experts into Dense Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Pruning and Distilling Mixture-of-Experts into Dense Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2605.28207v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is now the dominant architecture for frontier language models, yet it requires all expert parameters to be loaded in memory, making it less preferable for memory-constrained deployment. Existing compression methods reduce the number of experts but the output remains an MoE model with the same fundamental limitation. We present the first systematic framework for converting a trained MoE into a standard fully dense architecture: experts are scored, selected, and grouped, then concatenated into a dense FFN and refined by knowledge distillation from the MoE teacher. We evaluate 7 scoring, 5 grouping, and 2 magnitude scaling methods across a range of selected expert counts on Qwen3-30B-A3B, yielding 350 configurations. We find that the choice of scoring method is the most impactful, with our novel diversity-aware scoring consistently outperforming prior methods on Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, and GPT-OSS-20B. Under a controlled comparison at matched parameter count, MoE-to-dense outperforms dense-to-dense pruning by +6.3 pp in average downstream accuracy after ~4B-token distillation at 1.6x faster training wall-clock speed.

items.title: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Architecture to Output: Testing the Structural Origins of Hallucination and the Amplifying Role of Data
items.summary: arXiv:2606.07537v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surveys of hallucination classify errors by how an output relates to its source, and often explain them by the model's structure: attention retrieves by association, the maximum-likelihood objective has no term for truth, and left-to-right decoding commits to early tokens. Data, on this account, makes these failures worse rather than causing them. The account is usually argued rather than tested. We test it with interventions that need only sampling access. Study 1 holds pretraining data, tokenizer and scale fixed and swaps attention for a state-space mixer, using five Pythia/Mamba pairs from 130M to 2.8B parameters and four further attention models, on 111 facts presented with a planted false or a planted true statement. Swapping the mixer leaves free-recall failure unchanged (both 2.8B models answer 3 of 200 SimpleQA questions), but it changes what happens to a defect in the input. From 410M upwards, every attention model repeats the planted falsehood more often than its matched state-space model (2.8B: 650 vs. 566 of 666 items, p = 2.5e-20), also on facts both models know, while the state-space models can still read planted facts they did not know. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models. The correct fact cuts the share of answers with a downstream error from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works as well (p = 0.38), and the models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. The structural account survives in a narrower form. The mixing component decides whether a defect in the context becomes an output error, commitment decides how an error spreads, and on long-tail questions the first error comes from missing knowledge, not from a suppressed truth.

items.title: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Modeling Interventions can Modulate Emergent Misalignment
items.summary: arXiv:2606.23700v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) has been linked to the activation of misaligned persona vectors and evil character traits, suggesting that EM operates through disruption of the model's aligned character rather than direct learning of harmful content. Motivated by this connection, we study self-modeling interventions: specifically self-recognition and self-reports as character-targeted interventions that are distinct from existing in-training defenses. We conduct two-stage finetuning experiments across three models (GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct) and multiple EM datasets to compare self-recognition finetuning against benign finetuning baselines (correct domain-specific data, general knowledge, and word counting), finding it an effective defense in both reversal and prevention settings. For prevention, only self-recognition finetuning consistently reduces misalignment without exacerbating any individual metric, suggesting that character fortification specifically drives prevention. We also conduct in-training experiments across these models to compare the effectiveness of self-reports with benign interleaving and inoculation prompting. We provide further evidence for EM's relation to the LLM's default character by showing that EM finetuning leads to fragmentation of LLM's identity self-reports, reduces self-recognition performance to about chance, artificially corrupting self-recognition exacerbates misalignment caused by EM finetuning, and finetuning on self-reports from EM finetuned models can transfer misalignment. Together, these findings reframe EM not as the adoption of a coherent misaligned persona but as the destabilization of aligned character.

items.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2607.19181v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

items.title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
items.summary: arXiv:2608.09928v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exhibit strong visual understanding, yet the internal features that cause these behaviors remain difficult to identify, audit, or control. While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.

While applicable to post-hoc inspection, hidden states that are decomposed into interpretable feature directions using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) neither readily isolate which features are changed by multimodal training, nor are they directly useful for targeted control. We introduce MMDiff, a multimodal model-diffing framework that trains multimodal SAEs and turns them into feature-level interfaces for discovering and controlling multimodal behavior. MMDiff supports three uses: (i) feature isolation, by diffing a base-LM SAE against its multimodal-adapted counterpart to identify features altered by multimodal training; (ii) task-specific feature detection, via per-token contrastive firing analysis that isolates causal features; and (iii) feature-level control, by causally removing or steering the discovered feature directions. We train multimodal SAEs for three MLLM families, LLaVA-MORE, PaliGemma 2, and InternVL3.5, and evaluate on visual-spatial understanding, multimodal safety, and OCR. MMDiff discovers sparse, causally specific features whose removal selectively degrades target behaviors by an average of 12% on spatial tasks and 17% on OCR, and reduces attack success rate by 24% on multimodal safety attacks, with no impact on VQA performance. Steering these features improves spatial and OCR accuracy by +3.6% and +1.8% on average over a standard single-layer steering baseline. These results show that multimodal SAEs can serve not only as interpretability tools, but as mechanisms for auditing, steering, and controlling MLLMs behavior toward safer and more capable generations.

items.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36202v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Persona Selection Model (PSM) posits that post-training selects a persona the model learned during pre-training. Work on subliminal learning has shown that models can impart covert signals (like "love of owls") into semantically unrelated outputs like strings of numbers, and that students trained on these outputs inherit those traits. In this work I show that by evaluating the likelihood of such outputs under the base pre-trained model with an appropriate header, a method I call persona-header likelihood evaluation (PHLE), one can decode these subliminal signals and classify between them. For example, PHLE distinguishes number sequences generated by a post-trained model prompted with "You love owls" from those prompted with "You love trains", and distinguishes answers from a model with a secret desire to harm the user, filtered to remove any noticeable misalignment, from those of a model with no system prompt. In both cases prompted classifiers, including the generating model itself, perform far worse. The signal partially persists across model families, with the Qwen base model reading signals generated by Olmo and vice versa. This is evidence for a non-trivial prediction of the PSM, and the method may be practically useful for auditing the hidden objectives of models.

items.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
items.summary: arXiv:2611.06706v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

items.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
items.summary: arXiv:2611.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

items.title: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Should Diffusion Language Models Reconsider Their Commitments?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.11551v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) are well known for fast text generation via parallel decoding. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions, and less is known about how to selectively revise these early token commitments. In this work, we introduce $\underline{\mathrm{P}}$lanned $\underline{\mathrm{U}}$nmasking-and-$\underline{\mathrm{R}}$evision Joint $\underline{\mathrm{L}}$earning (PURL) for MDMs, a training-based framework that seamlessly unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. We derive a normalized joint transition whose likelihood factorizes into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction. These components are trained jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy. During inference, all three decisions are supported by a single shared forward pass, enabling the model to decode masked tokens and revise noisy tokens. Across logic puzzles, mathematical reasoning, and code generation, PURL improves accuracy at matched unmask budgets, with relative gains up to 47.4% accuracy improvement and up to an $8\times$ reduction in scheduled decoding rounds. Beyond these gains, our analysis further reveals general principles of revisable decoding: token edits become more effective as context accumulates; early edits can steer unfinished trajectories, whereas later edits tend to remain localized; and effective edits therefore depend on both calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise. Together, these suggest that effective parallel generation depends not on revising more tokens, but on making the right commitments revisable at the right time.

items.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
items.summary: Researchers have developed TopicScope, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to train causal topic classifiers capable of labeling the topic of each token in a model's generated response. Unlike previous activation-based monitors limited to detecting harmful content with few classes, TopicScope assigns topics dynamically throughout a response. Trained on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics, the classifiers demonstrated robustness to perturbations and generalized well across different model sizes. The study highlights that compact topic monitors can be efficiently trained during the prefill phase and deployed during generation, expanding the application of SAEs beyond safety classification. The associated code, dataset, and checkpoints are publicly available.

items.summary: A recent study investigated whether large language models internally represent psychological constructs or merely produce outputs resembling psychometric patterns. Using responses from Taiwanese university students and analyzing 14 variants of Llama 3 and Qwen models, researchers found that larger models replicate and amplify human psychological scale correlations. Internal geometric structures aligned with human data were observed in larger instruct models but not in base variants. The study also identified a phenomenon termed "readout attenuation," highlighting differences between internal model activations and behavioral outputs. Overall, the findings demonstrate decodability and alignment of psychological constructs within these models under specific assays, though they do not confirm that internal representations directly mediate observed behaviors.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
items.summary: A recent study explores the application of reinforcement learning techniques to optimize cancer chemotherapy treatment schedules. The research includes simulations using traditional Q-learning and advances to offline reinforcement learning methods, employing a model-based architecture with conservative Q-learning and offline policy optimization. Utilizing real clinical data from colon cancer patients, the proposed approach aims to generate optimal sequential treatment policies. Experimental results suggest that this model can effectively support junior oncologists in making treatment decisions.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
items.summary: A recent study reevaluated the performance of tabular foundation models (TFMs) against optimally tuned gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) for predicting customer churn in the telecom sector. Unlike previous benchmarks that compared TFMs to untuned GBDTs and focused solely on ranking metrics, this analysis considered profit-related metrics and calibration across five public telecom churn datasets. The results showed that the TabPFN-3.5 model achieved significantly higher expected maximum profit than the best tuned GBDTs on certain datasets, while other TFMs showed mixed results. The study also noted that licensing restrictions on TabPFN-3.5 weights currently limit its production deployment. Overall, the findings suggest that TFMs can offer advantages over tuned GBDTs in specific contexts, though further considerations such as licensing and dataset independence remain important.

items.title: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Seeing Is Not Believing: Counterfactual Lesion Erasure Teaches a Small Medical Vision-Language Agent to Report Only What the Image Shows
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) often report a finding because the question names it; standard benchmarks miss this. From public segmentation datasets we build counterfactual views without manual annotation: the lesion erased by inpainting, a same-shape control edit elsewhere, and unedited lesion-free images. The evidence sensitivity gap (ESG) is the rate of absent-or-refer answers after erasure minus the rate after the control edit; it is zero for a model that ignores the image or reacts to both edits alike. MedScope-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, LoRA, image tools) was trained on label-derived trajectories, selected by a pre-registered rule and tested once against nine frontier and six open VLMs; four pre-registered checks then probed the mechanism. On 507 internal cases across five imaging types, MedScope-4B reached ESG 0.758 and claimed an erased lesion in 9.6% of cases, against 0.27-0.47 and 41-62% for the frontier models (all p<0.001), without significant loss of accuracy on real lesions. Without counterfactual views ESG fell to 0.279+-0.107 (three seeds); the effect replicated on MedGemma 1.5 4B and two unseen inpainting tools. At four external centres the advantage held but frontier models detected more real lesions; on a fresh external test MedScope-4B detected 0 of 48 pneumothorax films, with net utility below gemini-4-argon's (-0.36 [-0.50, -0.23]). Matching the control edit was not shown to matter; over three seeds no fresh-external ESG advantage over removal-based DPO was established; a paired-view consistency objective did not beat a matched-compute control, while that continuation alone cut erased-lesion claims on unseen tools at every seed, at a cost in sensitivity at one. Training on erased and edited images gives a small model an evidence-gated disposition that prompting does not give frontier models; it does not improve perception, and rare critical findings need coverage.

items.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.13017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.

importance.development_summary: This research paper proposes Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), a new method for speculative decoding in language models that improves speed and accuracy by drafting multiple coherent token blocks simultaneously. MFD addresses inefficiencies in existing block drafting methods by reducing the creation of incoherent token prefixes called chimeras. Experimental results on Qwen models show significant speedups compared to prior approaches, indicating potential for more efficient inference.
